headline_en: How risky is the political role of the Bangladeshi diaspora
summary_en: Opinion column by Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder (North South University) arguing that the interim government formed after the 2024 uprising has brought overseas-resident and dual-citizen experts into key policy bodies, and that the diaspora should be welcomed for development but kept out of core political decisions. One section warns that most Bangladeshi expatriates are workers in the Middle East and Malaysia, where political activity by migrants is not tolerated and can lead to visa cancellation, blacklisting and closure of the labour market.

facts.statement: The column says that, according to the International Labour Organization ('ILO Migration Report 2023'), none of the Middle Eastern countries or Malaysia tolerates political activity by expatriates; doing politics there carries risks of visa cancellation, blacklisting and closure of the labour market.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, citing 'ILO Migration Report 2023'

facts.statement: The column states that the large majority of Bangladesh's expatriates are hard-working labourers in the Middle East and Malaysia (no figure given).
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder

facts.statement: The columnist warns that if political unrest spreads and Middle Eastern countries come to believe that Bangladeshi workers are getting involved in politics, those countries may stop issuing visas, and asks whether political demands such as voting rights for expatriates are more urgent than safe jobs and continuity of remittances.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder (his own opinion)

facts.statement: The column says the interim government formed after the 2024 mass uprising has included experts who live abroad or hold dual citizenship in many important state policy-making structures, some of whom have families living abroad, and that this has raised debate about transparency and 'dual loyalty'.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder

facts.statement: The column notes that India gives its diaspora 'Overseas Citizens of India' (OCI) status, which gives special economic opportunities but no political power or voting rights, and cites India and China as countries that used their diaspora for development while keeping them out of politics.
facts.source_in_article: Columnist, citing Devesh Kapur and Liu Hong / Els van Dongen

headline_en: Police of both countries coordinating on extradition of Bestinet's Aminul and Ruhul: Malaysian home minister
summary_en: Malaysia's home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said in Kuala Lumpur that Bangladesh's request to bring back Bestinet founder Aminul Islam Abdul Nor and his associate Ruhul Amin, accused of money laundering, is being handled through government-to-government and police-to-police coordination. The article recalls allegations that a syndicate in the Malaysian labour market laundered at least BDT 8,750 crore out of Bangladesh during the Awami League government, and that Bestinet runs the FWCMS system Malaysia uses to recruit foreign workers.

facts.statement: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail told journalists at an event in Kuala Lumpur that Bangladesh's request to return Bestinet founder Aminul Islam Abdul Nor and his associate Ruhul Amin, who are in Malaysia and accused of money laundering, is being settled through bilateral government (G-to-G) and police-level (P-to-P) coordination between the two countries.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, via Malay Mail quoting Bernama

facts.statement: It is alleged that at least BDT 8,750 crore was laundered out of Bangladesh during the Awami League government through a syndicate built in the Malaysian labour market; Bangladesh's manpower exporters claim that Bangladeshi-origin Malaysian citizen Aminul Islam and his Bangladeshi agent Ruhul Amin were the ringleaders, and they have submitted a memorandum asking the government to act.
facts.source_in_article: Allegation attributed to Bangladesh's manpower exporters; reporter's background

facts.statement: Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the matter was discussed with Bangladesh's Chief Adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus during Yunus's visit to Malaysia a few months earlier, and both sides agreed it would be settled through coordination at police level between the two countries. He gave no specific information on whether Dhaka had clarified the purpose of the extradition, saying 'for now this is all I can say'.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail

facts.statement: According to a report published 'last November', Saifuddin Nasution confirmed that Malaysia's home ministry had received a request letter from the Bangladesh government for the detention of Aminul Islam and Ruhul Amin; the letter said they face allegations of money laundering, extortion and trafficking of foreign workers.
facts.source_in_article: Earlier report cited by the article; Saifuddin Nasution

facts.statement: At that time Saifuddin Nasution said Malaysia had asked Dhaka for a clearer answer on the request: whether the purpose of detaining the two was extradition or further investigation, and whether it was to record the accused's statements or to conduct an investigation, which should first be made clear to Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail

facts.statement: The Malaysian government uses a system called the Foreign Worker Centralized Management System (FWCMS) to recruit foreign workers; the system is operated by the company Bestinet.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's background

facts.statement: Aminul Islam is the founder and chairman of Bestinet; the article says that although he has stepped down from the chairman's post he still holds a stake in the company.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's background

facts.statement: A related Prothom Alo headline linked in the article says members of BAIRA do not want a syndicate for sending workers to Malaysia and have submitted a memorandum to the ministry.
facts.source_in_article: Related-story headline printed in the article

headline_en: How the country's first 'Digital Island' sank
summary_en: Maheshkhali in Cox's Bazar was declared Bangladesh's first 'Digital Island' in 2017 under an IOM-funded project whose stated aims included preventing unsafe migration and human trafficking by sea. The project worked for about two and a half years, then collapsed for lack of oversight: 19 km of optical fibre was stolen, equipment was ruined or stolen, and distance-learning, telemedicine and e-commerce services stopped. The Department of Social Services, which took it over, has neither staff nor budget to restart it.

facts.statement: The 'Digital Island' project was launched in 2017 in Maheshkhali, Cox's Bazar (about 400,000 residents) with aims that included improving living standards, expanding education and business and preventing unsafe migration; it was implemented jointly by Korea Telecom, the Bangladesh government's ICT Division and Bangladesh Computer Council with financial support from the UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM), at a cost of BDT 22 crore 35 lakh 81 thousand.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's finding

facts.statement: Under the Maheshkhali Digital Island project, law enforcement agencies had taken an initiative to use high-speed internet to run operations at sea to stop human trafficking and arms and drug smuggling, in order to ensure safe migration.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's finding

facts.statement: The Digital Island project ran properly for the first two and a half years and then stalled; 19 km of optical fibre for the internet link was stolen, laptops, computers and projectors were ruined, and distance learning, telemedicine and e-commerce activities stopped. Internet at Adinath Government Primary School was cut in December 2019, and the ICT centre run by the Maheshkhali social services office was burgled on 13 October 2020.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's field visit; local teachers and officials

facts.statement: The project's ICT Training Centre was inaugurated on 25 January 2018 and handed to the Maheshkhali upazila Department of Social Services, which was to keep the project running but has not managed to in the last five and a half years; the Maheshkhali social services office has only two officers.
facts.source_in_article: Sources concerned; reporter

facts.statement: Md. Sofi Uddin, assistant director of the Department of Social Services, Cox's Bazar office, said the whole project collapsed during the Covid pandemic, restarting it would need everything including the optical fibre to be installed anew with a large budget the department does not have, and that for now they have moved to reopen the training centre and written to the director general for an allocation. The UNO, Md. Hedayet Ullah, said the computer training centre is to be reopened with the help of a private development organisation.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Sofi Uddin; UNO Md. Hedayet Ullah

headline_en: Those who do not enrol in college must also be thought about
summary_en: Prothom Alo editorial on the large number of SSC passers who did not even apply for class XI admission for 2025-26. It argues that jobs exist for young people at home and abroad but require training and technical knowledge, that opportunities for unskilled workers to go abroad have shrunk, and that the training offered by government and private bodies must be monitored.

facts.statement: The editorial says that previously large numbers of unskilled workers could go abroad with jobs but that opportunity has now shrunk considerably, and workers need at least minimum technical knowledge and training even to go abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul has said that some skill is now needed even to work in loading and unloading goods or in the construction and infrastructure sector.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul, as cited by the editorial

facts.statement: The editorial notes that some government agencies are training young people seeking jobs at home or abroad and some private institutions have grown up in response to demand, and says how much training the private ones actually give must be kept under watch.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: In 2025 there were 1,904,086 SSC and equivalent examinees, of whom 1,303,426 passed and more than 600,000 failed; about 10.75 lakh applied for class XI admission in colleges and madrasas for the 2025-26 academic year, and even after excluding about one lakh technical-stream passers, more than one lakh passers did not apply at all.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing Prothom Alo reports

headline_en: Five memorandums of understanding may be signed between the two countries
summary_en: Preview of Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus's three-day visit to Malaysia from Monday 11 August 2025, with a summit meeting with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Putrajaya on Tuesday. Five MoUs and three exchange notes (including one on higher education) may be signed. A senior foreign ministry official said removing the problems of Bangladeshis in Malaysia's labour market and taking more workers would get priority; expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul is in the delegation and Yunus will meet Bangladeshis living in Malaysia.

facts.statement: A senior Bangladesh foreign ministry official said that at the bilateral meeting between Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim (scheduled for Tuesday, the day after Yunus's arrival on Monday 11 August 2025, in Putrajaya), removing the problems faced by Bangladeshis in Malaysia's labour market and Malaysia taking more workers would be given importance.
facts.source_in_article: A senior foreign ministry official, to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: During Yunus's three-day visit to Malaysia starting Monday 11 August 2025, five memorandums of understanding and three exchange notes may be signed: MoUs on defence cooperation; energy cooperation including LNG and petroleum supply and infrastructure; BIISS-ISIS Malaysia cooperation; cooperation between the Bangladesh-Malaysia Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BMCCI) and chip maker MIMOS; and FBCCI with a Malaysian business body. None of the listed MoUs is on labour.
facts.source_in_article: Diplomatic sources

facts.statement: The three possible exchange notes between Bangladesh and Malaysia are on the halal ecosystem, the two countries' foreign service academies, and cooperation in the higher education sector.
facts.source_in_article: Diplomatic sources

facts.statement: On Tuesday afternoon of the visit Yunus was scheduled to join an exchange-of-views event with Bangladeshis living in Malaysia; the delegation includes expatriates' welfare and overseas employment adviser Asif Nazrul, foreign adviser Md. Touhid Hossain, energy adviser Muhammad Fouzul Kabir Khan, national security adviser Khalilur Rahman, special envoy Lutfey Siddiqi and BIDA executive chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter

facts.statement: Bangladesh has long been trying to become a 'sectoral dialogue partner' of ASEAN, and Malaysia's prime minister is the current ASEAN chair, so Dhaka hopes for a positive result; Anwar Ibrahim visited Bangladesh 'last October', the first head of government to visit after the interim government took office on 8 August 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Senior foreign ministry official; reporter

facts.statement: On Wednesday of the visit Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia was to confer an honorary doctorate on Yunus at a special convocation.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter

headline_en: Japanese language course, admission fee only one thousand taka

The notice gives eligibility, 50 seats, a BDT 1,000 assessment fee, how to get and submit the form, selection priorities and the full admission timetable.

facts.statement: Bangladesh-Korea Technical Training Centre opened admission to a Japanese language (Level N4) course, run under the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment and designed specially for workers who want to go to Japan. headline_en: What is in the NCP's 24-point 'Second Republic' manifesto
summary_en: National Citizen Party (NCP) convener Nahid Islam announced a 24-point 'Manifesto for a New Bangladesh' at the Central Shaheed Minar on Sunday 3 August 2025. Most points concern the constitution, justice, governance, health, education and the economy, but point 15 pledges training and certification for exporting skilled manpower, point 18 pledges recognition and legal protection for migrant workers, and point 22 sets out pledges on expatriates' voting rights, harassment-free embassy and airport services, body repatriation, an emergency fund and reintegration. These are party promises, not government measures.

facts.statement: On 3 August 2025 the National Citizen Party (NCP) convener Nahid Islam announced a 24-point manifesto at a rally at the Central Shaheed Minar; point 22 is titled 'Dignity and rights of expatriate Bangladeshis'. These are a political party's pledges.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 22 pledges that if an expatriate worker dies the party will arrange for the body to be brought home without harassment and give the family all kinds of support, and that it will work to ensure expatriate workers' healthcare and overall welfare.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 22 pledges voting rights for expatriates, harassment-free service at embassies and airports, an emergency assistance fund, safe investment at home and digital government services for expatriates.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 22 pledges rehabilitation and dignified employment arrangements for expatriates who return home or fall into crisis, firm steps to prevent human trafficking and protect the interests and human rights of Bangladeshi citizens abroad, and creating scope for expatriates to take part directly in state policy-making.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: The NCP manifesto refers to 'more than one and a half crore' expatriates who it says played an outstanding role in the July mass uprising, and pledges state recognition of that contribution.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 15 pledges special emphasis on IT, healthcare, nursing, management, logistics, hospitality and engineering for exporting skilled manpower abroad, with enough training centres to teach sector- and country-specific skills and languages.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 15 pledges to widen training and certification in technical trades for skilled manpower export and to take joint initiatives with foreign certification bodies to bring them to international standard.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: The NCP manifesto states that Bangladesh has about 30 lakh unemployed people, two of every three of them young.
facts.source_in_article: NCP convener Nahid Islam, reading the party's 24-point manifesto

facts.statement: NCP manifesto point 18 pledges recognition and legal protection for all workers, explicitly including migrant, domestic, agricultural, transport, informal and self-employed workers, and a 'permanent labour commission'.

headline_en: Three detained in Malaysia on suspicion of militancy have returned and are being questioned: Asif Nazrul
summary_en: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said on Friday 4 July 2025 that three of the Bangladeshi workers arrested in Malaysia over alleged militant links have already returned and are being questioned, and all who return will be questioned and tried if evidence is found. Earlier that day Malaysia's police chief Khalid Ismail said 36 Bangladeshis were detained for spreading Islamic State ideology and raising funds among workers: 5 charged, 15 to be deported, 16 still in custody.

facts.statement: Malaysia's Inspector-General of Police Khalid Ismail told a press conference in Kuala Lumpur on Friday 4 July 2025 that 36 Bangladeshi nationals had been detained for alleged militant links; of them 5 have been charged with being members of a terrorist organisation, 15 will be sent back to Bangladesh, and 16 remain in police custody under investigation.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian police chief Khalid Ismail, via Reuters

facts.statement: The Malaysian police chief said authorities had broken up a ring of Bangladeshi workers that used social media and online messaging platforms to spread Islamic State (IS) ideology among workers, recruited other Bangladeshi workers and collected funds; the detained workers sent money to the IS group in Syria and Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian police chief Khalid Ismail, citing intelligence, via Reuters

facts.statement: Khalid Ismail said 100 to 150 people are believed to be involved in the ring; those with a low level of involvement will be sent back to their own country, those deeply involved will be dealt with under Malaysian law, and operations to catch suspects will continue.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian police chief Khalid Ismail

facts.statement: Adviser Asif Nazrul said on the night of Friday 4 July 2025 that three of those arrested in Malaysia had already returned to Bangladesh and were being questioned; everyone detained on this allegation who returns will be questioned, and if evidence of militant involvement is found, by Bangladesh itself or from Malaysian authorities, they will be put on trial.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul, to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said Malaysia is a friendly state where 'several lakh' Bangladeshis work, that such allegations against a few are very embarrassing and a concern for both countries, and that Bangladesh is in contact with Malaysia at a high level and will take a tough stand against militancy.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul

facts.statement: The article says Malaysia relies heavily on foreign manpower for factories, plantations/farming and construction, and that thousands of Bangladeshi nationals go there for work every year.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's background (Reuters)

headline_en: 36 Bangladeshis arrested in Malaysia on allegations of militant involvement
summary_en: Malaysia's home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail confirmed on Friday 27 June 2025 that police arrested 36 Bangladeshis for alleged direct involvement in a 'radical militant movement' in a three-phase operation in Selangor and Johor that began on 24 April. Five have been charged with terrorism-related offences, 15 have been issued deportation orders and 16 are still under investigation.

facts.statement: Malaysian police arrested 36 Bangladeshis on allegations of direct involvement in a 'radical militant movement'; the operation was carried out in three phases from 24 April (2025) in Selangor and Johor, as confirmed by home minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail on Friday 27 June 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail (statement)

facts.statement: Five of the 36 arrested Bangladeshis were charged under what the article calls 'section 6A of Malaysia's Penal Code', applicable to terrorism-related offences, at the sessions courts in Shah Alam and Johor Bahru.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail

facts.statement: Of the remaining arrested Bangladeshis, 15 have been issued orders of expulsion (deportation) from Malaysia and further investigation is continuing against the other 16.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail

facts.statement: The minister said police Special Branch intelligence showed the group was inspired by Islamic State (IS) ideology and had formed a cell within its own community to radicalise members, raise money for terrorist activity and work to overthrow the legitimate government of their home country.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail

facts.statement: Malaysia's home minister said Malaysia will never be allowed to become a shelter for any foreign extremist group or a safe base for anti-state conspiracies, and that swift, strict action will be taken against any such attempt.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail

headline_en: Travel ban on 12 people including Nizam Hazari and Meher Afroz Chumki
summary_en: On Sunday 25 May 2025 Dhaka Metropolitan Senior Special Judge Md. Zakir Hossain, on separate Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) applications, banned 12 people from travelling abroad. Ten of them are linked to the ACC's inquiry into charging more than the government-fixed amount for manpower export to Malaysia and laundering money abroad, including former MP Nizam Uddin Hazari and owners or managing directors of several recruiting firms. The other two, former state minister Meher Afroz Chumki and her husband, face an unrelated illegal-wealth case.

facts.statement: On 25 May 2025 Dhaka Metropolitan Senior Special Judge Md. Zakir Hossain imposed a foreign travel ban on 10 people connected with the Malaysian labour market, after the ACC told the court it is inquiring into allegations of collecting money in excess of the government-fixed amount for manpower export to Malaysia and laundering money abroad, and had learned that these 10 were trying to flee abroad.
facts.source_in_article: ACC submission to court; court order

facts.statement: The people banned from travel in the Malaysia labour-market inquiry are, as printed: Nizam Hazari and his wife Nurjahan Begum; Snigdha Overseas Limited owner Sheikh Abdullah and M Amirul Islam; Catharsis International Limited managing director Mohammad Ruhul Amin; Messrs Unique Eastern Limited managing director Noor Ali, Nasir Uddin Ahmed and Khondaker Shawkat Hossain; BM Travels chairman Shafiqul Islam; and BNS Overseas Limited managing director Engineer Ishtiaque Ahmed. (The wording does not make clear which firm M Amirul Islam, Nasir Uddin Ahmed and Khondaker Shawkat Hossain belong to.)
facts.source_in_article: Court order as reported

facts.statement: In a separate matter the same court banned former state minister Meher Afroz Chumki and her husband Mohammad Masudur Rahman, former chief executive of Bangladesh Petroleum and Lubricants, from travelling abroad until investigation ends in an ACC case alleging BDT 2 crore 31 lakh of wealth beyond known income; this case is not about migration.

headline_en: Four kg of gold recovered by burning the clothes of two Bangladeshis returning from Dubai
summary_en: Two Sylhet men working in Dubai, Mohammad Shajahan and Alim, were arrested on 25 April 2025 at Dhaka and Sylhet airports wearing underwear and vests coated with gold, from which customs recovered more than four kg by burning the garments. Shajahan, who needed gallbladder surgery, had been offered his travel costs by a man named Ziaur Rahman in return for carrying 'valuables'. Both are in jail under the Special Powers Act and police are trying to identify the ring behind Ziaur.

facts.statement: On 25 April 2025 customs arrested Dubai returnee Shajahan at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, and Alim the same day at Osmani International Airport, Sylhet; more than four kg of gold was recovered by burning the clothes they were wearing, and both are in jail in a case under the Special Powers Act.
facts.source_in_article: Customs authorities; Airport police

facts.statement: The gold was hidden as a coating inside garments: in a fifth-floor room of a multi-storey building in the Deira area of Dubai, where four or five other men from Sylhet were already present, Ziaur Rahman gave Shajahan and Alim three pairs of underwear and three vests each to wear, photographed them, and told them to land very carefully because 'their man' at the airport would find them on arrival.
facts.source_in_article: Investigators, citing interrogation; Airport police inspector Rafiqul Islam

facts.statement: Recruitment of the carriers: Shajahan was found to have gallstones, learned that surgery in a Dubai hospital would cost more than BDT 2 lakh, and decided to have it done in Bangladesh; Ziaur Rahman of Gowainghat, Sylhet then offered to pay his travel costs to and from Bangladesh if he carried Ziaur's 'valuable goods', saying he would be told what it was when he left. Shajahan and Alim sent passport photos and their own photos to Ziaur's WhatsApp number and Ziaur bought their air tickets.
facts.source_in_article: Investigators, citing interrogation

facts.statement: Both men flew from Dubai on the same flight (printed as 'Bangladesh Airlines'), which landed at Sylhet after 10 am, where Alim got off and was arrested by customs on prior information; he named Shajahan, who was arrested with intelligence-agency help when the aircraft landed at Dhaka at about 11:15 am.
facts.source_in_article: Customs authorities

facts.statement: Customs recovered 2 kg 417 g of gold from Shajahan's garments, which were cut into pieces and burned for 8 hours, after which the gold was separated from the ash; the complainant customs officer said it took about 24 hours in all to separate the gold after his arrest (the article gives both 8 hours and about 24 hours). Gold dust was recovered from Alim's clothes in the same way.
facts.source_in_article: Customs assistant revenue officer Baki Billah (name spelled two ways in the article)

facts.statement: Airport police station questioned Shajahan on seven days' remand from 26 April to 2 May 2025 in the Special Powers Act case; investigating officer Inspector Rafiqul Islam called Ziaur Rahman one of the ringleaders of gold smuggling and said conversations and messages with Ziaur found on Shajahan's phone are being checked to identify the ringleaders.
facts.source_in_article: Airport police station inspector Rafiqul Islam

facts.statement: Mohammad Shajahan, 38, of Dewar village, Gowainghat, Sylhet went to Dubai four years earlier and sent his monthly earnings home; Alim, from the same area, also went to Dubai for work.
facts.source_in_article: Customs authorities and Airport police

headline_en: Religious affairs ministry asks people not to perform Hajj without a permit
summary_en: In a government handout on Friday 2 May 2025 Bangladesh's religious affairs ministry asked Bangladeshis at home and in Saudi Arabia not to perform Hajj without a permit, not to stay in Makkah or the holy sites on visit visas during the Hajj season, and not to sponsor, transport or house violators. It sets out the Saudi rules for 29 April to 10 June 2025: fines up to SAR 20,000 for pilgrims without a permit, up to SAR 100,000 for helpers, vehicle confiscation, deportation and a 10-year entry ban.

facts.statement: Under new rules issued by the Saudi government for the 2025 Hajj, entry into Makkah is prohibited without a valid permit from the relevant authority to work in the holy sites, proof of residence (iqama) registered in Makkah, and an officially issued Hajj permit.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh government handout (Ministry of Religious Affairs), citing Saudi rules

facts.statement: The Saudi government said the rule is in force from 1 Zilqad (29 April) to 14 Zilhajj (10 June) 2025: in this period no one may enter or stay in Makkah city or the surrounding holy sites without Hajj permission, and people who entered Saudi Arabia on visit visas will be under the highest level of surveillance.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi government, as cited in the Bangladesh government handout

facts.statement: Saudi Arabia's interior ministry said anyone who tries to perform Hajj without a Hajj permit will be fined up to 20,000 Saudi riyals; anyone who helps faces a fine of up to 100,000 Saudi riyals, and if the offence is proved the helper's own vehicle will be confiscated by court order.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi interior ministry, as cited in the Bangladesh government handout

facts.statement: The Saudi government said any foreign national who overstays or tries to perform Hajj without valid permission will be expelled from the country and barred from entering Saudi Arabia for the next 10 years.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi government, as cited in the Bangladesh government handout

facts.statement: Bangladesh's Ministry of Religious Affairs instructed Bangladeshis not to stay in Makkah or Saudi Arabia's holy sites on a visit visa during the current Hajj season, and asked Bangladeshis in Bangladesh and in Saudi Arabia not to perform Hajj without a Hajj permit.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Religious Affairs, government handout of 2 May 2025

facts.statement: The ministry asked Bangladeshis to refrain from sponsoring visit-visa holders who break Hajj rules, transporting them, helping them enter the restricted Hajj area, or arranging accommodation for them in hotels or homes.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Religious Affairs, government handout of 2 May 2025

facts.statement: Religious affairs adviser A F M Khalid Hossain said about 35 lakh Bangladeshis are working in Saudi Arabia and the highest remittance comes from Saudi Arabia, and that everyone should refrain from acts that would harm relations between the two countries.
facts.source_in_article: Religious affairs adviser A F M Khalid Hossain, in the government handout

facts.statement: A related Prothom Alo headline printed in the article says the fine for performing Hajj without permission is BDT 15 lakh.
facts.source_in_article: Related-story headline printed in the article

headline_en: Satisfaction with immigration and many other services at Shahjalal airport, but dissatisfaction too
summary_en: A field report from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on Saturday 8 March 2025. Returning and departing migrants said immigration now takes minutes rather than a long wait, luggage arrives quickly, and the Probashi Lounge opened on 11 November offers a good environment and cheaper food. Complaints remain: the 24 e-gates installed two and a half years ago mostly do not work, Wi-Fi is unreliable, and immigration police say they are short of staff, work on equipment from 2014 and have faulty passport readers and document detectors.

facts.statement: The interim government opened a 'Probashi Lounge' for the country's migrant workers at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 11 November (2024). On 8 March 2025 the reporter saw 15-20 passengers there, talking with relatives, eating food bought from the adjacent shop and charging mobile phones.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's visit

facts.statement: A worker at the Probashi Lounge food shop, Provati, said arrangements have been made so expatriates can buy food at low cost; Kuwait-based Alif Hossain said the lounge environment is much better than elsewhere in the airport and the food comparatively cheaper.
facts.source_in_article: Food shop worker Provati; expatriate Alif Hossain

facts.statement: Rayhan, a construction worker in Abu Dhabi since 2012, said that when he returned on 24 September he completed immigration and got his luggage within 15 minutes, and that on Saturday 8 March 2025 the whole departure immigration process at Shahjalal airport took about 10 minutes, whereas earlier it took a long time.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriate Rayhan

facts.statement: Alif Hossain of Bancharampur, Brahmanbaria, who has lived in Kuwait since 1996 and travels every three months, said he finished immigration at Shahjalal airport in one minute on Saturday 8 March 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriate Alif Hossain

facts.statement: Sharmin Shiri, who arrived from the United States on the night after 1 March 2025, said immigration took 10-15 minutes and luggage came quickly, but she could not use the Wi-Fi; passengers from Singapore who landed at 5:30 pm on 2 March said they finished immigration and had their luggage before iftar.
facts.source_in_article: Passengers interviewed

facts.statement: On average 150 flights take off and land at Hazrat Shahjalal airport per day, and police complete immigration (arrival and departure) for an average of 28,650 passengers a day.
facts.source_in_article: Immigration police sources

facts.statement: From 1 December to the afternoon of Saturday 8 March 2025, Shahjalal airport immigration police processed arrival immigration for 1,337,856 passengers of 204 countries and departure immigration for 1,469,695 passengers of 199 countries.
facts.source_in_article: Shahjalal airport immigration police data

facts.statement: From 'last September' to Saturday 8 March 2025 the immigration police Document Analysis Centre detected 46 fake visas, 5 residency cards, 4 fake/tampered passports and 30 impostors (people using another person's passport details with their own photo).
facts.source_in_article: Immigration police

facts.statement: Besides processing outbound passengers, immigration police detain passengers on the 'stop list' (people with a ban or objection on leaving the country), seize forged travel documents, issue visas on arrival and collect fines for expired visas.
facts.source_in_article: Immigration police sources

facts.statement: Shahjalal airport has 12 e-gates each at arrival and departure (24) plus two VIP e-gates, 26 in total; they were launched two and a half years ago and were supposed to complete an e-passport holder's immigration automatically in 18 seconds, but the reporter found most gates not working and most passengers reluctant to use them.
facts.source_in_article: Staff on duty at the e-gates; reporter's observation

facts.statement: Two passengers said the e-gates are effectively useless: after passport data is verified at the e-gate, the passenger still has to complete immigration through the same process as everyone else.
facts.source_in_article: Two passengers interviewed

facts.statement: Immigration police at Shahjalal airport have 48 counters at arrival and 42 at departure; more than 500 police work in four shifts around the clock, 125-130 per shift. They worked three shifts before and moved to four shifts after 5 August (2024), but a staff shortage remains.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter; people concerned

facts.statement: The computer equipment used for the immigration software system dates from 2014 and no longer works properly; the passport readers mostly cannot read a passport in one go and sometimes need 7-8 attempts, wasting passengers' time.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter; immigration police

facts.statement: An immigration police officer said each shift was given 10 'document and bank note detectors' about two months earlier, but most have already become unusable, which makes it hard to detect fake passports or visas.
facts.source_in_article: An immigration police officer, anonymous

facts.statement: Special Branch chief Md. Golam Rasul said visa on arrival will from now on be given online with payment made on reaching the airport, and that within one to two months payment by card from abroad will also be possible, as part of automating the whole process.
facts.source_in_article: SB chief Md. Golam Rasul

facts.statement: SB Special Superintendent of Police (Immigration Operations) A K M Akhtaruzzaman said automation is being prioritised so passengers do not wait long and the aim is to make immigration paperless; desk officers' duty allocation and some other functions have already been automated.
facts.source_in_article: SB Special SP (Immigration Operations) A K M Akhtaruzzaman

facts.statement: In January and February (2025) 18,151 Chinese nationals arrived in Bangladesh and 18,308 left; immigration police say 99 percent of them understand no language other than Chinese, so officers need language training.
facts.source_in_article: Immigration police sources

facts.statement: Immigration police say they have no food arrangement inside the airport and must buy food at high prices, lack enough transport, and desk officers' chairs are not ergonomic.
facts.source_in_article: Immigration police sources

headline_en: Expatriates in Malaysia spend a holiday in the land of clouds and hills
summary_en: A reader-contributed piece about 70 Bangladeshi expatriates in Malaysia who, connected through social media, took two buses from Kuala Lumpur to Cameron Highlands in Pahang state to mark International Mother Language Day. It says Bangladeshi workers are seen at all the tourist spots there and dominate work in the vegetable farms.

facts.statement: The writer says Bangladeshi workers are found at every tourist spot in Cameron Highlands, Pahang state, Malaysia, and that the vegetable farms in particular are overwhelmingly worked by Bangladeshis.
facts.source_in_article: Reader-writer of the 'Dur Porobash' piece

facts.statement: The writer claims that similarities in weather, food habits, religion and culture make Malaysia a top choice for Bangladeshi workers and that Bangladeshis are now the largest group in Malaysia's labour market (no figure given).
facts.source_in_article: Reader-writer of the 'Dur Porobash' piece

facts.statement: On the occasion of International Mother Language Day, 70 Bangladeshi expatriates from different places in Malaysia who connected through social media travelled in two buses from Kuala Lumpur, leaving before sunrise and reaching Cameron Highlands at 9:30 am.
facts.source_in_article: Reader-writer of the 'Dur Porobash' piece

facts.statement: Prothom Alo's 'Dur Porobash' section accepts expatriates' stories, event news, videos, photos and writing by email at dp@prothomalo.com.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo notice at the end of the piece

key_quote_bn: বিশেষ করে বলতে হলে সবজির বাগানগুলোতে একচেটিয়া বাংলাদেশিদের আধিপত্য।
